passages.title: Motion Pictures
passages.text:
Most writings on the subject of motion pictures, including those scrutinizing the structural characteristics, aesthetic qualities, and effects of motion pictures on audiences, have traditionally been relatively abstract and have not considered what a filmʼs audiences actually see. In fact, various external factors intervene between the filmmakerʼs intent and the audienceʼs experience, often altering the qualities of a film and, consequently, the viewerʼs perception of it.

In the process of distribution, a film can be mutilated in many ways. The damage is most obvious when films in one language are shown to audiences that speak a different language. Subtitling may be simply incompetent, full of mistakes, or used for actual censorship. Dubbing—a significantly more profound intervention—can be even more damaging. Some films are reedited to render them “more understandable” by their target audiences, while others are given new titles rather than translations of their original titles, a practice that often creates false expectations and distorts the works intent.

When a film is shown on television or video, it suffers the most extensive deformations. In addition to causing a loss of image size and definition, current mass-market television and video technology is harmful in other ways. These intrusions include advertisements that break the intended continuity, the superimposition of images—such as station identifications and weather bulletins—over parts of the picture, and spoken announcements over parts of the soundtrack considered by programmers to be “unimportant.” Some alterations, such as a subtle increase in the projection speed of a televised movie to obtain more commercial time, are almost imperceptible but nonetheless detrimental to the integrity of a film.

It seems that audiences and even most film critics have tacitly accepted this situation—they rarely speak about it. This may be partly because of the special nature of film. In many other arts it is obvious that reproductions of a work are not the work itself, and they are not treated as such. However, the very nature of film makes it an exactly reproducible art form; under ideal conditions, each print is not merely a reproduction but is in fact another instance of the work itself. But we tend to overlook how rarely the ideal conditions apply, and this is disturbing for two reasons. First, professional analysis, interpretation, and evaluation may be unfair to filmmakers when—as is surprisingly often the case—they are based on a version that has already been seriously altered. Second, when criticsʼ comments are based on original, uncompromised versions of the films, they may raise false expectations with regard to the more or less faulty versions that are often available to viewers.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The impact of distribution and presentation on the integrity and perception of motion pictures.

**Framework**

Problem / Solution

**Main Point**

The way films are distributed, translated, edited, and especially shown on television or video often alters the intended experience, yet this is rarely acknowledged—creating problems for both audiences and critics. **Most Valuable Sentence:** The last paragraph, especially: “Professional analysis, interpretation, and evaluation may be unfair to filmmakers when—as is surprisingly often the case—they are based on a version that has already been seriously altered. Second, when criticsʼ comments are based on original, uncompromised versions of the films, they may raise false expectations with regard to the more or less faulty versions that are often available to viewers.”

**P1: The Usual Approach Overlooks the Audience’s Real Experience**

Most discussions and analyses of movies ignore what audiences actually see, focusing too much on abstract qualities. But lots of outside factors come between what the filmmaker intends and what the audience ultimately experiences.

**P2: Specific Ways Distribution Alters Films**

Distribution can seriously change films, especially with foreign films. Subtitles and dubbing can introduce errors, censorship, or big changes. Sometimes films are re-edited or given new titles that misrepresent their original intent.

**P3: Television and Video Transformations**

When movies are shown on TV or video, they're altered even more. Not only do you lose picture quality and size, but you get commercials, on-screen graphics, and interruptions that mess with the flow. Other changes, like slightly speeding up a film to allow more ads, are subtle but still damaging.

**P4: Why This Problem Is Overlooked—and Why It Matters**

People (including critics) mostly ignore these problems, maybe because film feels like a perfectly reproducible art form. But perfect conditions are rare, and this overlooks two big issues: (1) critiques of films are often based on already-altered versions, which is unfair to directors, and (2) when critics review the original versions, they can give audiences misleading expectations about what’s actually available.

questions.prompt: In the passage, the author primarily attempts to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The author's first sentence clues us in on the author's agenda. Any time the early sentences stress what has *usually / typically / mostly* been the case, it's setting us up for a contrast.

"Most writings have not considered what a film's audiences actually see", so the author is going to darn well consider what a film's audience actually sees!

Why does the author care about this?

She thinks it's totally unfair to the artistic vision of the filmmaker when adulterate films by changing the audio or the speed or the title, etc.

It feels like the author is trying to turn the spotlight on an overlooked **problem**: we've gotten to accustomed to doin' these filmmakers dirty by showing compromised / altered versions of their work and acting like it's the real work.

The author doesn't really provide any **solutions**. She just ends by articulating the two reasons the status quo is "disturbing".

So let's look for something like "alert the world to the problem (of how we alter films without appreciating the extent to which we're tarnishing their aesthetic value).

choices.text: provide evidence against a claim that is often made in the criticism of a particular art form
choices.tag: Out of Scope: evidence against a claim
choices.explanation:
The author seems to have her own agenda. She's here to complain about the ways in which we tolerate alterations of film.

The central purpose of this passage is not **reacting against** some claim.

(This answer feels more like a *Challenge Position* passage, but this passage seems more like a *Problem w/o Solution*).

choices.text: establish that changing the materials used in a particular art form would enhance public appreciation of that art form
choices.tag: Unsupported Causal Claim / Unrelated to Goal
choices.explanation:
This looks nothing like *Call Out a Problem*. It feels more like *Make a Recommendation*.

Where in the passage did the author say that "if filmmakers change the materials they're using, it would enhance public appreciation of film"?

The author's agenda was to enhance film appreciation (by the public and by critics) by encouraging us to preserve the original film as intended. There's nothing about "changing materials".

choices.text: refute a commonly held view regarding the detrimental effects of criticism on a particular art form
choices.tag: Out of Scope: refute a view
choices.explanation:
The author seems to have her own agenda. She's here to complain about the ways in which we tolerate alterations of film.

The central purpose of this passage is not **reacting against** some view.

(This answer feels more like a *Challenge Position* passage, but this passage seems more like a *Problem w/o Solution*).

choices.text: describe a problem that is generally overlooked in the criticism of a particular art form
choices.explanation:
"Describe a problem" certainly aligns with our *Problem w/o Solution* framework. The author wrote this passage to complain about the ways in which we tolerate alterations of film.

Is that a problem that's "generally overlooked"?

Yes! The very first sentence says that "most writings have not considered what audiences actually see" (i.e. they haven't considered that what audiences see is often an adulterated version of the original film)

choices.text: explain why a particular art form is the target of negative criticism
choices.tag: Out of Scope: explain why it's criticized
choices.explanation:
The author is here to complain about the ways in which we tolerate alterations of film.

This answer sounds like she was offering a *Causal Explanation* for why film is the target of negative criticism.

There's no part of the passage where it sounds like "the art form of film" is negatively criticized.

The closest we get to that is in the second to last sentence, where the author suggests that "since we ignore these alterations that have taken place before an audience sees the film, we are often unfairly subjecting films to critical judgment based on some altered form, not the actual work the filmmaker created and intended."

But that has nothing to do with saying that "the art form of film is the target of negative criticism".

questions.prompt: The author distinguishes film from at least some other art forms with regard to the

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
The author distinguishes film from other art in the last paragraph.

Many art forms have reproductions that are obvious reproductions, not the work itself, and not treated as the work itself.

Film, ****however****, is so exactly reproducible under ideal conditions, that "prints are not merely reproductions, but in fact another instance of the work itself".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Look for an answer saying something like "film is different with regard to the potential for a reproduction to be more than just a reproduction, but an actual instance of the work itself"?

Stay grounded in this Support Window. Force the answer to be reinforcing what we were told in the sentences where the author names a contrast between films and other art forms.

choices.text: extent of public reliance on professional analyses and evaluations
choices.tag: Out of Scope: reliance on pro analysis
choices.explanation: There's nothing in this Proof Window about either art form relying on professional analysis.

choices.text: possibility of creating multiple instances of the same artwork
choices.explanation:
This is talking about what the Proof Window is talking about --- with other forms of art, it's obvious that reproductions of the work are not the work itself.

With films, because it's exactly reproducible, each print is in fact another instance of the work itself.

With films, it's possible to create multiple instances.
With these other art forms, it's not possible.

(the strength of "not possible" might scare us, but this is the most supportable answer. If reproductions in these art forms are ****obviously**** not the work itself, it suggests that it's not the type of thing that can be actually replicated very well at all)

choices.text: susceptibility of the artwork to damage through environmental factors and aging
choices.tag: Out of Scope: damage through aging
choices.explanation: Nothing in this Proof Window says anything about environmental damage and aging.

choices.text: degree of control that a workʼs creator has over the conditions of its public presentation
choices.tag: Out of Window: control of presentation
choices.explanation:
We talked a lot about the myriad ways that films will be presented that betray the filmmaker's intentions (out of their control), but this moment of the passage that the question stem is pointing us to doesn't say anything about this.

The author never distinguishes film from other forms of art on this level.

choices.text: complexity of the methods used to provide public access to artwork
choices.explanation: This window of text, and the passage overall, doesn't really talk about how ****complex**** the method of providing public access to film, or other works of art, is.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since this has an *Undefined Target* we can head straight to the answers, or we can briefly remind ourselves of the author's main points (not that the correct answer has to necessarily test one of those).

The author is trying to raise awareness about the fact that alterations made to a film (subtitles, dubbing, new titles, superimposed images, adjustments to speed, scenes cut, changing image size, etc.) are betraying the filmmaker's vision.

Let's be wary of answers with any of the famous trap qualities:
- Too Strong
- Unsupported Comparison / Causality
- Out of Scope
- Opposite

choices.text: Films should be projected at precisely the speed at which they were designed to be projected.
choices.explanation:
While the extreme language of "precisely the speed at which they were designed" is an initial turn-off, this author **is** a stickler for trying to faithfully represent the original vision of the filmmaker; that's the main point of the passage.

The final sentence of the 3rd paragraph is our support:

*Some alterations, such as a **subtle increase in the projection speed** of a televised movie to obtain more commercial time are almost imperceptible but nonetheless **detrimental to the integrity** of a film.*

Since the author thinks that "subtle increases" are detrimental, he would insist that the film be projected at precisely the intended speed.

choices.text: Filmmakers should accept the fact that criticisms are often directed against distributors rather than against filmmakers.
choices.explanation:
The second to last sentence of the passage goes against this answer. It sounds like the author is concerned that criticisms will be directed against the filmmaker, not the distributor:

*Professional analysis, interpretation, and evaluation may be unfair to filmmakers when - as is surprisingly often the case - they are based on a version that has already been seriously altered.*

choices.text: Film critics should acknowledge that mutilations of films during distribution and public exhibition are inevitable.
choices.explanation:
This flies in the face of the author's main point. He is sending out a warning to the world that is saying, "It sucks that we tolerate all these mutilations of the filmmaker's actual intended artistic output".

He does not want to just accept this with resignation; he wrote the passage in order to rail against it.

So he wouldn't say, "we should just accept that these mutilations are inevitable." He'd be more likely to say "we should stop doing these mutilations" or maybe something like "film critics should appreciate that the work they're judging may have been subject to mutilations."

choices.text: Film commentaries should not be concerned with audience reactions to films.
choices.explanation:
The first sentence of the passage is a complaint:

*most writings (commentaries) on film have traditionally **not** considered what a film's audiences actually see*.

This sentence isn't exactly about audience reactions to films, but it reflects the fact that the author thinks that film commentaries should be taking into account the audience's perception of the film.

Even if this doesn't seem like counterevidence undermining this answer, we still wouldn't be able to find any support text that matches this answer. The author never chastises film commentaries for worrying about audience reactions to a film.

choices.text: Films should be viewed only in relatively large, darkened theaters.
choices.explanation:
The author never says anything about the size or lighting of viewing conditions.

The author wants the actual film to be as close to the original as possible in terms of sound / aspect ratio / speed / title / visuals.

But if a "director's cut" of a movie (i.e. a copy in which none of those things were changed) were to be shown in a small screening room at a library or some rich person's house, this author wouldn't have any strong objections.

This is simply too restrictive an idea, especially given that the author never emphasized viewing conditions such as "dark room + pretty big theater".

questions.prompt: Which one of the following would, if true, most strengthen the author's argument concerning any modification of a film for distribution?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
If we CTRL + F "modification", we won't find it. If we search for "distribution", we'll find it in the first sentence of the 2nd paragraph.

That 2nd paragraph lists a few ways that films get adulterated / modified / "mutilated" in the distribution process.

But the question stem is asking us to strengthen the author's **argument** about these modifications that occur in the distribution process. That means we should try to identify what we think we could call the author's *Conclusion* in regards to this topic.

She doesn't like them. Again, "mutilated" is not a neutral choice of verb, for a list of modifications / alterations / edits / truncations / adaptations.

How are these seemingly minor changes **mutilating** (i.e. destroying / defiling) these films?

The author's evidence is essentially:
- we should try harder to show the "correct" version of the film that the artist created, given that film is a medium that allows us to do such a thing

- there may be more of a disconnect between critics and audiences (the critic unfairly dislikes a film because they see an edited version, or the critics like the early version of a film and recommend it to audiences who then see the crappier edited version).

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
There no focused conclusory language about film modifications, so we should just think to ourselves, "Our author doesn't like these modifications because each one is a betrayal of the artist's intended work, and the author thinks we should be properly consuming *that* intended work."

Let's find an answer that aligns with / intensifies that point of view.

choices.text: Almost all filmmakers whose work critics respect approve of the distribution of altered versions of their films.
choices.explanation:
This answer is saying, "more than 90% of the best filmmakers approve of alterations to their film through the distribution process".

So, author, you can keep complaining and objecting that these alterations are *mutilating* these films, but almost all of the filmmakers themselves (the ones you would care the most about) are totally fine with it.

choices.text: Mass-market television and video technology has recently improved in its ability to present films in ways that conform to the intentions of filmmakers.
choices.explanation:
The author is trying to sound the panic alarm about how bad it is when we modify films during distribution. She hates this practice, because it's a betrayal of the artist's vision and final product.

But this is tamping down that concern, saying, "Yeah, it was worse in the past, but it's not as much of a problem any more. Nowadays, we do a better job of conforming to the filmmakers' intentions, so chill out, Author."

choices.text: Many professional commentaries on nonfilm artworks are based on aged, mutilated, or otherwise altered versions of those works.
choices.explanation:
If anything, this feels like a Weaken answer, but it's very weak in strength, so it has little impact overall.

Our author is worried about altered versions of cinematic artworks, because it's unfair to the filmmaker for a critic to judge an altered version of the film.

This answer is sort of saying, "Relax, author, this happens in a lot of fields of art, not just film. It's common for professional criticism to be based on an altered, even mutilated, version of the work."

choices.text: Almost all viewers of films are unaware of the professional commentaries that are written about those films.
choices.explanation:
The final sentence of the passage shows the author worrying that audiences will be given false expectations because the critic saw a different version of the film than they will see.

But if, as this answer says, audiences are almost always unaware of what the critics have said, then there's no harm to fear.

choices.text: In almost every film that has a soundtrack, all parts of the soundtrack are designed by the filmmaker to contribute significantly to the filmʼs artistic value.
choices.explanation:
There's no way we could have predicted this specific answer, but it does underscore one of the author's concerns.

In the middle of the 3rd paragraph, the author laments that there are sometimes "spoken announcements over parts of the soundtrack considered by programmers to be 'unimportant'."

Is that really such a big deal, author? Do we really need to be concerned if the station hypes the new episode of "Young Sheldon" during the opening music of *Shawshank Redemption*?

Yes, say the author and this answer choice: *because **all** parts of the soundtrack are designed by the filmmaker to contribute **significantly** to the film's artistic value*.

This helps strengthen the author's case that these alterations we're doing when we modify for distribution are corrupting/mutilating the artwork.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that the author believes which one of the following statements about films?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since the entire passage is about "films", it seems hard to narrow the Support Window here.

We can briefly remind ourselves of the author's main points about film, although the correct answer won't necessarily be testing that.

She is clearly a purist who wants the film we watch to be identical to the film the filmmaker considered the finished work.

Don't change the play speed, the image size, the soundtrack, the title, etc. Maintain the artist's original vision and choices.

Let's find the most supportable answer, which will probably reflect that notion that "any changes we make to the film are bad / they're a betrayal of the filmmaker's specific vision".

choices.text: When shown on television—even without having been reedited and without any commercial breaks or superimposed messages—films can be artistically compromised to some extent.
choices.explanation:
We're drawn to this answer with its "come hither" soft language:

*Films **can** be compromised to **some** extent when shown on TV*.

Are there any things we do to films shown on TV beyond the excluded categories of "re-edited / commercial breaks / superimposed messages"?

Yes! The second sentence of the 3rd paragraph says,

*In addition to causing a loss of image size and definition, current mass-market television and video technology is harmful in other ways.*

That sentence implies that "loss of image size and definition" is one way in which TV technology is harmful. And 'harmful' is understood here to mean "deformations / mutilations of the artist's final product", so any harm is artistically compromising to some extent.

choices.text: Films are considered by many art critics to be of questionable significance as a topic of serious scholarly analysis, interpretation, and evaluation.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: not worthy of serious analysis
choices.explanation:
The author definitely thinks that art critics often fail to appreciate how the subtle changes that happen to a film before it's seen by critics are unfairly deforming the original work.

But the passage never suggests that many art critics don't even consider film to be a topic of serious scholarly analysis.

choices.text: Because of technical limitations involved in the process of reproducing films, no reproduction of any one film can be strictly classified as the work that the filmmaker intended.
choices.explanation:
The final paragraph says,

*The very nature of film makes it an **exactly reproducible** art form; under ideal conditions, each print is **not merely a reproduction** **but** is **in fact** another instance of **the work itself.***

choices.text: Even when they are distributed in uncompromised versions, films elicit variable responses from viewers, and thus they can rarely be expected to have the aesthetic impact that the filmmakers intend.
choices.tag: Too Strong: rarely have intended impact
choices.explanation:
The whole passage is talking about all the ways in which we compromise films by the time they are seen by viewers.

This answer is talking about a case we really don't discuss -- what happens when viewers see the *uncompromised* versions.

And it says a pretty strong idea for which we have no textual support: *even when an audience sees the film exactly as the filmmaker intended, the aesthetic impact is rarely what the filmmaker intended*.

choices.text: Most films do not meet the standards set by writings that analyze their structural and aesthetic qualities.
choices.tag: Too Strong: most / Out of Scope: standards set by writings
choices.explanation:
This answer combines strong language, "**more than 50%** of films", with an unmentioned concept "the standards set by writings that analyze films".

We don't know anything about what "standards" are set by writings, and we have not idea what percentage of films meet those standards.

questions.prompt: Suppose that a Russian company is planning to distribute to Russian-speaking audiences a film that was produced in Italy with dialogue originally spoken only in Italian. It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following recommendations regarding the film?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
What would this author tell the Russian company to do with this Italian language film?

In the beginning of the 2nd paragraph she addresses what can happen "*when films in one language are shown to audiences that speak a different language*":

- subtitling may be incompetent
- subtitling may be used for censorship
- dubbing, a ****significantly more profound**** intervention, can be even more damaging
- a new title, that isn't a direct translation, may create false expectations

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
The author hates all this stuff, because she wants everyone to see something that is as close as possible to the original version of the film. But she probably understands that if a Russian audience saw the original Italian version, they'd be totally lost.

So she'd probably try to make the best of it
- don't dub, since that's the worst
- subtitle, but don't censor and make sure you competently translate
- keep the title like the original (translate it, but don't change it)

choices.text: The company should attempt to translate the filmʼs title into Russian but should also make explanatory material available for audiences that know no Italian.
choices.explanation:
Why, if we're translating the title into Russian, do we ****also**** need explanatory material available for audiences that know no Italian.

We're already assuming our Russian audience doesn't know Italian, which is why we translated the title into Russian.

This is essentially a mixed bag answer that doesn't make a ton of internal sense, and the *explanatory material* doesn't match up with anything from the passage.

Our author might be more likely to say, "Keep it all in its original Italian form, but make explanatory material available for audiences that don't know Italian".

choices.text: The company should first make the film available only to critics who understand Italian and afterwards should release it to the general public.
choices.explanation:
The harsh, restrictive recommendation of "****only**** let critics who know the language see it first, ****then**** release it to the public" doesn't match up with anything from the passage.

The author never talked about a staggered release schedule, where it first goes to people who know the language and then goes to those who don't.

choices.text: The film should be subtitled in Russian, but only if the translation is strictly faithful to the original.
choices.explanation:
This matches up with two of the 2nd paragraph's ideas:

- the author hates it when subtitling is done incompetently, full of mistakes, or when it is used for censorship (so she would agree that the translation should be as faithful to the original as it can be).

- the author thinks dubbing is worse than subtitling (so she would agree that we should subtitle, rather than overdub new Russian actors saying these lines in Russian)

choices.text: The version of the film that Russian-speaking audiences see should not include subtitles.
choices.explanation:
We know from the 2nd paragraph that the author thinks dubbing "can be even more damaging" than bad subtitling. So we can't pick this answer thinking, "The author would agree. She'd rather it be overdubbed in Russian than for it to be subtitled."

If we're picking this answer, we'd be thinking that the author would rather the film not have subtitles or be dubbed. But how would Russian-speaking audiences get enough out of the movie if they couldn't understand any of the dialogue?

The author's main concern was trying to let these films, as works of art, be experienced by audiences in a way such that the viewer's perception of the film is closest to what the filmmaker intended.

We can use our common sense to surmise that filmmakers intend for the dialogue in their films to be understood by the audience. So it would be a pretty out there film critic if she were insisting, "Sorry! You have speak Italian or else just follow along by looking at the images and guessing what all the characters are saying."

The author never specifically bad-mouthed subtitles, just incompetent mistake-ridden subtitles or subtitles that omit certain parts of the dialogue for the sake of censorship.

choices.text: The film should be very cautiously restructured, as needed, to make the filmmakerʼs intentions clearer to Russian-speaking audiences.
choices.explanation:
While the goal of this answer is noble (making the filmmaker's intentions clearer to Russian-speaking audiences), it's a pretty far-fetched recommendation to say, "Here, Russian company. Here is a completed Italian film. Go head and very cautiously restructure it."

This author is deeply uncomfortable when anyone besides the original filmmaker is messing with the film, so entrusting a Russian company to restructure an Italian filmmaker's film sounds riskier (in terms of drifting from the filmmaker's intent) than does just adding accurate subtitles.

passages.title: Fish Farming
passages.text:
A recent worldwide decline of ocean fishery stocks has stimulated rapid growth in cultivated production of fish and shellfish, usually known as fish farming. Between 1987 and 1997, for example, global fish production from farming doubled. Fish farming produces a quarter of all fish and shellfish eaten by humans, and, as global population increases, fish farming will probably become even more important in supplying human protein needs. Some experts even argue that in addition to helping to compensate for the decline in ocean harvests, fish farming will restore wild populations by relieving pressure on ocean fisheries. There is, however, little if any evidence that fish farming will restore ocean fishery stocks. The complexity of production systems leads to an underlying paradox: fish farming is a possible solution, but also a potential contributing factor, to the continued decline of ocean fishery stocks worldwide.

In the first place, the more intensive forms of fish farming, oriented toward high-volume production, threaten the sustainability of ocean fisheries through water pollution and ecological disruption. Intensive fish farming usually involves the enclosure of fish in a secure system; population densities are typically high, resulting in the generation of large amounts of waste and increased potential for the spread of pathogens. Habitat destruction through the spread of untreated waste, the escape of species not native to the farmʼs region, or contamination by new pathogens can all ensue, seriously damaging ocean and coastal resources and, ultimately, wild fishery stocks.

Even more important, intensive farming of many species of fish requires large inputs of fish meal and fish oil in order to supply fatty acids that vegetable matter lacks or essential amino acids that it inadequately supplies, like lysine and methionine. For the ten species of fish most commonly farmed, an average of 1.9 kilograms of wild fish is required for every kilogram of fish produced. Of the ten species, only three—catfish, milkfish, and carp—require less fish input than is eventually harvested, while the farming of carnivorous species like salmon has a very high input-to-output ratio. Although some defenders of fish farming contend that predatory carnivores in the wild consume even more fish than they would on a farm, farming of such carnivorous species requires up to 5 kilograms of wild fish for every kilogram of fish produced.

Expanding farm production does have the potential to alleviate some of the pressure on wild fishery stocks. For example, increasing the farm production of fish like salmon can reduce prices, deterring investment in fishing fleets and, over time, reducing fishing efforts. Similarly, other farmed fish like tilapia and channel catfish provide alternatives to ocean fish like cod and haddock. Nonetheless, even these benefits may in the end be lost because niche markets have started to develop for several species of wild-caught fish, causing their catch rates to remain high even as the production of viable farmed substitutes has increased.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The impact of fish farming on global ocean fishery stocks

**Framework**

Problem / Solution

**Main Point**

While fish farming has grown rapidly and seems like a solution to declining wild fish stocks, it is also part of the problem due to pollution, ecological disruption, and heavy reliance on wild fish as feed. So, fish farming is both potentially helpful and harmful for ocean fisheries.
**(The "Most Valuable Sentence" appears at the end of the first paragraph: "...fish farming is a possible solution, but also a potential contributing factor, to the continued decline of ocean fishery stocks worldwide.")**

**P1: The Rise and Paradox of Fish Farming**

Fish farming is booming as ocean fisheries decline and now supplies a large portion of seafood eaten by people. Some believe it could save wild fish stocks, but there’s not much proof—it might help, but could also make things worse.

**P2: Environmental Impacts of Intensive Fish Farming**

High-density fish farming can cause big problems: it pollutes waterways, spreads diseases, and lets non-native species escape, all of which can hurt wild fish populations and damage natural habitats.

**P3: Reliance on Wild Fish as Feed**

Many farmed fish, especially carnivores like salmon, need to eat a lot of wild fish to grow—often more than the resulting harvest. This means that farming some species puts even more pressure on wild fish stocks.

**P4: Potential Benefits and Their Limitations**

Fish farming can lower prices and reduce the commercial pressure on wild fish by offering alternatives. However, the demand for wild-caught specialty fish still remains high, so the benefits may be limited.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the main point of the passage?

choices.text: The recent decline of ocean fishery stocks was caused by damage to ocean habitats resulting from fish farming.
Fish farming has some potential both for increasing global fish supplies and for threatening those very supplies.
Fish farming is destined to supply ever-larger percentages of human protein needs.
The high catch rates for several types of wild-caught fish overshadow the advances made by fish farming.
Because of their diet, carnivorous fish are more expensive and difficult to farm than noncarnivorous fish.

questions.prompt: There is information in the passage sufficient to answer which one of the following questions?

choices.text: How does the escape of species not native to a farmʼs region result in habitat destruction?
choices.explanation:
The only mention of habitat destruction comes at the end of the 2nd paragraph.

We're told that habitat destruction can occur through the spread of untreated waste, through the escape of species not native to the farm's region, or through contamination by new pathogens.

But it never dives into that 2nd detail to explain *how* the escape of non-native species can lead to habitat destruction. It only says *that* the escape of non-native species can lead to habitat destruction.

choices.text: What sort of shellfish is most commonly raised on fish farms?
choices.explanation:
*Shellfish* is only covered in the 1st and 3rd sentences of the passage, but no specific types of shellfish are ever named.

(Shellfish are like shrimp, crabs, lobsters, etc.)

choices.text: Approximately how many kilograms of fish, on average, does a wild salmon consume during its lifetime?
choices.explanation:
The 3rd paragraph is the only time hear about *kilograms* of fish.

We know that salmon has a very high input-to-output ratio (you have to feed salmon between 1.9 - 5 kg of wild fish for each 1 kg of salmon you produce).

But we don't know how heavy the average salmon is, so we can't apply this ratio to anything in order to derive an answer to this question.

If we produce a 10kg salmon, then it apparently consumed 19 - 50 kg of wild fish.

If we produce 5kg salmon, then it consumes 10-25 kg of wild fish in its lifetime.

choices.text: What proportion of the fish and shellfish eaten by humans is produced on fish farms?
choices.explanation:
*Shellfish* is only mentioned in the 1st and 3rd sentences of the passage, and in the 3rd passage it says that,

*Fish farming produces* *****a quarter***** *of all fish and shellfish eaten by humans*.

So 1/4, or 25%, of the fish and shellfish eaten by humans is produced on fish farms.

choices.text: How long does it take for niche markets for wild-caught fish to have an appreciable effect on wild populations?
choices.explanation: *Niche markets* are only discussed in the final sentence of the passage, and that sentence doesn't give us any way to derive how long it takes for niche markets to have an appreciable effect.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is closest to the meaning of the phrase "relieving pressure on ocean fisheries" as used in the middle of the first paragraph?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The sentence in which this phrase appears is saying that fish farming can do 2 things:

1) make up for the "budget shortfall" of fish from the *decline in ocean harvests*.

In other words, if the world is used to eating 50,000 tons of fish every year, but because of declining ocean harvests (i.e. because less fish are being caught out of the ocean), we only caught 40,000 tons of fish this year. The fish we acquire from fish farming can supply that missing 10,000 tons of fish.

2) *restore wild population by relieving pressure on ocean fisheries.*

There are fewer fish in the ocean than there used to be (a worldwide decline of ocean fishery stocks). If we were to stop fishing in the ocean for a little bit (or to fish less), and got our fish from fish farms instead, we would give the ocean fish a little reprieve, so that they could have lots of babies and grow their populations back to the levels they used to be at.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: In that sense "relieving pressure on ocean fisheries" just means "we won't need to grab as many fish out of the ocean / we'll give them time to replenish their numbers".

choices.text: making up for the scarcity of wild-caught fish
choices.explanation:
This answer is referring to the first half of the sentence. The #1 thing we listed above. Making up for the scarcity of wild-caught fish is saying, "the world, in 2021, demands 50,000 tons of fish per year, but because there aren't as many wild fish to catch, we only caught 40,000 tons. How are we going to make up for that missing 10,000 tons of fish so that we can meet the seafood demand of the world in 2021?" This is a short-term problem that fish farming can help.

When the passage is talking about "restoring wild populations by relieving pressure on ocean fisheries", it's referring to a long term problem where fish farming can help.

If we do a lot more fish farming for the next ten years, then maybe by 2030, the fishery stocks in the ocean will have built back their numbers to where they used to be.

choices.text: supplementing the incomes of people who make a living from ocean fishing
choices.explanation: This phrase has nothing to do with the incomes of people who do ocean fishing. It's just saying, "we won't be grabbing as many fish out of the ocean (thus they'll have some time to build back up their population to old numbers)."

choices.text: causing fewer wild fish to be caught
choices.explanation:
This phrase meant something like, "we won't be grabbing as many fish out of the ocean (thus they'll have some time to build back up their population to old numbers)."

By using fish farming more and more, we'll use ocean-fishing less and less, causing fewer wild fish to be caught, thereby relieving pressure on depleted ocean fisheries.

choices.text: reducing the amount of income to be earned from ocean fishing
choices.explanation:
This phrase is not referring to the income of people who do ocean fishing. It's just saying, "we won't be grabbing as many fish out of the ocean (thus they'll have some time to build back up their population to old numbers)."

Yes, it's true that if we're doing less ocean fishing, then the amount of income earned from ocean fishing will probably be reduced. But the meaning of "relieving pressure on ocean fisheries" is not "reducing the amount of money that ocean fishermen make".

choices.text: reducing overall demand for fish and fish products
choices.explanation:
The phrase "relieving pressure on ocean fisheries" is not referring to an attempt to reduce ****overall**** demand for fish. We're redirecting where we get our supply of fish. We're not changing demand.

But getting more of our supply from fish farms, we need to acquire less fish from the ocean, which will put less pressure on depleted ocean fisheries.

This answer would be fine if it said, "reducing demand for fishing fleets to catch fish from the ocean".

questions.prompt: The information in the passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: No *Clue Words*, so nothing to look for.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Distance ourselves from toxic-looking answers:
- Too Strong
- Out of Scope
- Goes Against Passage
- Unknown Comparisons

Try to find a moderately worded claim and then see if we can match it up with support text or with the author's gist.

choices.text: Any further decline in ocean fishery stocks would not be caused entirely by human activities.
choices.explanation:
This language is super soft and lovable, so we should give this answer a good chance.

To support that "any further X would not be caused entirely by Y", we would just need to be able to say that "a further instance of X would be caused in part by Z"?

Can we say that a further decline in ocean fishery stocks will be caused at least in part by something unrelated to human activities?

We don't have anything in the passage that sounds like a nonhuman cause of decline to ocean fishery stocks.

choices.text: The best way to reduce the price of wild-caught fish is to put a farmed variety of the same species on the market.
choices.tag: Too Strong: best / Unknown Comparison / Goes Against Passage
choices.explanation:
Not only is this way too strong to be derivable (the passage does not rank all the different ways to reduce the price of wild-caught fish), it is somewhat undermined by the very end of the passage.

It says that putting a farmed variety of salmon on the market can reduce prices of wild-caught salmon, deterring investment in fishing fleets and efforts to get wild-caught salmon.

But then the passage says, "nonetheless, even these benefits may in the end be lost". That doesn't sound like rousing praise for "the best way".

choices.text: If fish farming does not continue to increase, then it is unlikely that worldwide human protein needs can be met.
choices.explanation:
This answer could be rephrased, "In order for world protein needs to be met, we will probably have to continue increasing fish farming."

Our author isn't even a big fan of fish farming, so it would be weird for him to be communicating that it's likely to be essential to meeting worldwide protein needs.

We were told that fish farming "will probably become even more important in supplying human protein needs",

choices.text: Most consumers do not perceive a difference in taste between wild-caught and farmed varieties of the same species of fish.
choices.tag: Too Strong: most / Out of Scope: consumer perception / Unknown Comparison
choices.explanation: The passage never talks about consumers' perceptions of farmed vs. wild fish. We don't know whether most people can perceive a difference or not.

choices.text: The use of wild fish to meet the nutritional needs of farmed fish could result in the overfishing of worldwide fish stocks.
choices.explanation:
This answer reflects the gist of the 3rd paragraph. We won't find its essence contained in any one sentence, but instead in the structural logic of the passage.

The end of the 1st paragraph is saying,

"Fish farming is a possible solution, but also **a potential contributing factor**, to the continued decline of ocean fishery stocks worldwide".

The 2nd paragraph discusses one reason why fish farming can contribute to the decline of worldwide ocean fishery stocks:

"**In the first place** ... fish farming can hurt fishery stocks via pollution and ecological disturbance"

Then the 3rd paragraph discusses another reason why fish farming can contribute to the decline of worldwide ocean fishery stocks:

"**Even more important** ... fish farming involves feeding those fish 1.9 kg of wild fish for ever 1 kg of farmed fish produced."

So the 3rd paragraph is saying that this "net loss" we experience through fish farming (we spend 1.9 kg of wild fish to get 1.0 kg of farmed fish) is the more important reason why fish farming is a potential contributing factor to the continued decline of ocean fishery stocks worldwide.

questions.prompt: The views put forward in the passage conform most closely to which one of the following principles governing new methods of food production?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This is a tough question stem to parse at first. It sounds way broader than the fish farming topic of the passage.

Is there a new method of food production in this passage?

Yes the first sentence tells us about a "****recent**** worldwide decline of ocean fishery stocks stimulating rapid growth in ... fish farming".

How does our author feel about fish farming?

She seems pretty ambivalent, saying in her thesis at the end of the first paragraph that it's "a possible solution, but also a potential contributing factor, to the continue decline of ocean fishery stocks worldwide".

So one principle, from her negativity there, could be that "a new method of food production shouldn't contribute to the very problem it was invented to ameliorate".

In the 2nd paragraph, the author gets more specific about water pollution and ecological disruption. These are examples of how the new method of food production is worsening the situation for fish in the ocean.

The 3rd paragraph stresses that an even bigger problem with this new method of food production (fish farming) is that the fish input is larger than the fish output. You need to feed the fish being farmed 1.9 kg of wild fish, just to get out 1 kg of farmed fish.

The 4th paragraph is full of a couple positives and a negative.
- good that increasing supply via fish farming can lower fish prices which lowers incentives for fishing fleets to grab wild fish

- good that some farmed fish reduce consumer demand for other types of ocean fish

- bad that wild-caught fish is now a trendy item that some people will pay lots for, increasing the incentives for fishing fleets to find them.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
We basically want to find a principle that says one of the things the author complained about, in relation to fish farming, is something that new forms of food production should avoid.

Or it could potentially connect one of the good things the author said about fish farming to a principle about what new forms of food production should ideally do.

choices.text: They should be employed only if they do not result in major changes in consumer demand for foods produced using traditional methods.
choices.explanation:
The contrapositive of this is saying,

*if a new method of*
*food production results then that new food*
*in major changes in → production method*
*consumer demand shouldn't be used*
*for traditional foods*

This trigger doesn't match any of the complaints the author made. In fact, we might consider consumers' switching from wild cod and haddock to farmed tilapia and catfish to be a major change in consumer demand, and that was actually one of the things the author *liked* about fish farming.

choices.text: They should be employed if they are economically more efficient than existing methods and their use will not result in business failures or loss of jobs.
choices.explanation:
This rule says:

*if a new method*
*of food production then that new*
*is more economically → food production*
*efficient and method should*
*won't result in be used*
*business failures*
*or lost jobs*

This trigger doesn't match either of the compliments the author made. In particular, she never talked about whether businesses would fail or jobs would be lost as a result of fish farming.

Also, it would be peculiar if we ended up picking a principle that says "we ****should**** employ this new method", since it felt the author overall has more misgivings than encouragement.

choices.text: They should not be employed if they will ultimately result in a net decrease in food of the type produced.
choices.explanation:
This rule says:

*if a new method of*
*food production will then that new food*
*ultimately result in → production method*
*net decrease of should not be used*
*that type of food*

This trigger matches the discussion in the 3rd paragraph, in which we learned that it takes between 1.9 - 5 kg of wild fish to get 1 kg of farmed fish.

Based on that input / output ratio, the practice of fish farming is resulting in a net decrease of fish.

Of course, this answer is being a little bit "cute" in the sense that if a fish farm's type of food produced is understood as *salmon*, then it's not fair to say that fish farming salmon results in a net decrease in salmon produced.

But if you define this simply as *fish*, then the author did establish that fish farming will result in a net decrease in fish (as a product in human markets, not on the planet).

choices.text: They should be employed if they promote diversification in the types of foods available for human consumption and help to bring about environmental improvement.
choices.explanation:
This rule says:

*if a new method of*
*food production then that new food*
*promotes food → production method*
*diversification should be used*
*and brings about*
*environmental*
*improvement*

This trigger doesn't match either of the compliments the author made. The author mentioned that people would switch from wild cod/haddock to farmed tilapia/catfish. But swapping these 2 for those 2 isn't really diversifying the types of food available for consumption.

And the author definitely does *not* think that fish farming improves the environment. To the contrary, the 2nd paragraph told us that fish farming has some bad effects on the environment.

Also, it would be peculiar if we ended up picking a principle that says "we ****should**** employ this new method", since it felt the author overall has more misgivings than encouragement when it comes to this new method.

choices.text: They should be employed only if they replace other methods that have undesirable ecological effects.
choices.explanation:
The contrapositive of this is saying,

*if a new method of food*
*production doesn't then that new food*
*replace other method → production method*
*that had undesirable should not be used*
*ecological effects*

This trigger doesn't match any of the complaints the author made. She never said, "ocean fishing didn't have any undesirable ecological effects, thus fish farming should not be employed".

The author speaks of fish farming *relieving pressure* on wild fishery stocks, so it's implied that wild fishing was putting pressure on wild fishery stocks (an undesirable ecological effect). In fact, it may even be that wild fishing has contributed to the worldwide decline of ocean fishery stocks, which is an undesirable ecological effect.

questions.prompt: The statements in the passage provide the most support for the view that the author believes which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The only keyword we have to go off is "the author", so we have a few options:

1. Head into the answers, distance ourselves from stuff that's Too Strong or making an Unknown Comparison, and research answers with weaker or ruling-out language.

2. Briefly remind ourselves of the author's main opinions

3. Go hunting for specific sentences that had attitudinal language or felt more like where the author's voice was most concentrated in the passage.

The author's main opinions were that fish farming had some advantages, but it looked like they had some pretty serious disadvantages also. He wasn't convinced it was a net gain or a net loss, but he was challenging the position of people who seem *overly excited* about the prospects of fish farming being our saving grace.

The author's voice was pretty constant after his initial "However" pivot in the first paragraph, so we probably wouldn't try to hunt for specific opinion moments.

choices.text: Most farmed fish are carnivorous.
choices.explanation:
The overly precise modifier *most* is dangerous in Reading Comp (and on Necessary Assumption and Most Supported in LR). Can we get that precise? Do we know that more than 50% of farmed fish are carnivorous?

The end of the 3rd paragraph mentions carnivorous fish that are farmed (such as salmon), but it never says that they're more than 50% of farmed fish.

choices.text: Farmed and wild fish consume the same foods.
choices.tag: Too Strong: same / Opposite, if anything
choices.explanation:
The concept *same* is very dangerous in Reading Comp (and Necessary Assumption and Most Supported in LR).

If we said the word "identical" instead, it would sound as extreme as it is.

The passage actually suggests, in the 3rd paragraph, that farmed fish are eating some *unnatural* diet of vegetable matter that doesn't supply enough vitamins, so they add fish meal and fish oil (which would never be found in the wild) to the diet of the farmed fish.

choices.text: Pollution is currently more damaging to wild fish populations than is overfishing.
choices.explanation:
We have no way to tally up all the damage points inflicted by pollution and all the damage points inflicted by overfishing and measure them against each other.

And the passage never makes a comparative judgment about which one causes more damage overall.

choices.text: Market forces can either encourage or discourage overfishing of ocean fisheries.
choices.explanation:
When we say "X is either Y or Z" we mean that "at least one of Y and Z" is true about X.

So technically you can support this being a true claim as long as you can support encourage ****or**** discourage.

But they had in mind dual support, because the author was listing a lot of different pros and cons.

In one way, farm fishing is good:
The 2nd sentence of the final paragraph explains that as fish farming increases for salmon, there will be more salmon supply on the market, so the market price of salmon will go down, which will deter people who might otherwise have thought to invest in wild salmon fishing.

Kathleen was thinking, "Is the big money in salmon fishing fleets?" and was thinking about investing her inheritance in that sector, until she looked into the numbers and saw that the profit margins were razor thin, now that fish farming has lowered the price consumers are expecting to pay for salmon.

Because Kathleen decides to *not* invest in a fishing fleet, it "reduces fishing efforts", which allows wild fisheries to build back their population. Market forces discouraged Kathleen from overfishing ocean fisheries.

In the final sentence of the passage, market forces encourage overfishing. Niche markets open up for wild-caught fish ... people go on anniversary dinners to eat their $500 / bowl of shark fin soup.

The fact that rich people lust for the forbidden fruit of these wild caught fish means that economic incentives to go fishing for them remain: "*causing their catch rates to remain high even as the production of viable formed substitutes has increased".*

choices.text: The market for wild-caught fish is likely to remain a small one.
choices.explanation:
When the author talks about the market for wild-caught fish in the last sentence, she doesn't sound optimistic, like "no worries ... the market is likely to remain small".

Instead, she's saying "even these benefits may in the end be lost!" because of these niche markets.

She isn't necessarily saying the market will become a medium sized one, but we have no touchable support for this optimism that it will remain small.

The tone of this sentence is "PIVOT back into pessimism and alarm".

questions.prompt: The information in the passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There's nothing to go off here, so let's head to the questions.

Let's be wary of common trap answer forms:
- Too Strong/Specific
- Unknown Comparisons
- Out of Scope
- Opposite / Goes Against

choices.text: Wild fish require different nutrients than farmed fish do.
choices.explanation:
The 3rd paragraph talks about what we feed to farmed fish. If anything, it seems to suggest that farmed fish need similar types of nutrients to what wild fish do.

We're trying to give farmed fish a diet of vegetable matter, but we realize that it's not good enough. After all, (both wild and) farmed fish need fatty acids and need ample amounts of lysine and methionine.

choices.text: It is more profitable to farm species such as catfish, milkfish, and carp than to farm species such as salmon.
choices.explanation:
We know that one category of expenses is lower for catfish, milkfish, and carp, compared to salmon. For the former trio, for every 1 kg of fish meat we get, we need to feed them less than 1 kg of fish meal. For salmon, for every 1 kg of fish meat we get out, we need to feed them around 5 kg of fish meal.

So we spend more money feeding salmon than we do this other power trio of fish. But this answer is about ****profit****, which is "Revenue - Expenses". So even if the expenses for catfish / milkfish / carp are lower than those for salmon, we won't know which is more profitable until we find out how much revenue salmon brings in compared to these other three.

We probably know we've paid a pretty penny for a plate of salmon at a nice restaurant, whereas we're less likely to have paid the same for catfish / milkfish / carp.

choices.text: The farming of tilapia and channel catfish produces as much environmental damage as the farming of cod and haddock.
choices.explanation:
It's very extreme to say that the farming of tilapia and catfish produces ****equal**** damage to what the farming of cod and haddock produce.

In the final paragraph, it's mentioned that farmed fish like tilapia and catfish can provide alternatives to ocean fish like cod and haddock. We don't have any information about ****farming**** cod and haddock.

And there's no way from that one sentence that we could derive how the overall environmental damage of farming each pair of species compares.

choices.text: A growing number of consumers are choosing wild-caught fish of certain species in preference to farmed fish.
choices.explanation:
This is supported by the final sentence of the passage:
*Niche markets* *****have started to develop***** *(*a growing number of consumers*) for several species of wild-caught fish.*

The last sentence was essentially warning that as we make more and more of our fish come from fish farming, some people will be like, "I want ****ocean-caught**** fish, and I'll pay extra for it", which then creates an incentive for fishing fleets to get back out there.

choices.text: Noncarnivorous fish in the wild typically do not consume more food than their farmed counterparts do.
choices.tag: Too Strong: typically / Unknown Comparison: wild vs. farmed
choices.explanation:
The 3rd paragraph only talks about *carnivorous* fish, by name. It's implied that catfish / milkfish / carp are noncarnivorous, though.

Does the wild version of these fish consume more food than their farmed counterparts do?

We have no idea. We never compare the dietary intake of wild catfish to farmed catfish, for example.

And even if we did, it would be a stretch for us to generalize from any of these three species to a statement about what's ****typical**** for wild, noncarnivorous fish in general.

questions.prompt: The author of the passage would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements regarding pollution caused by fish farming?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We have some *Clue Words*, "the pollution caused by fish farming". The 2nd paragraph is where the author most directly dealt with pollution:

- the more intensive the operation, the more it's oriented toward high-volume production, the more likely we'd be to see pollution as a result.

- water pollution usually happens within the farm's water, given the density of the fish populations swimming in there (a lot of waste and increased potential for pathogens).

- it also speaks to the fact that habitats can be destroyed through the spread of untreated waste / pathogens

- species can escape from a farm into a local ecosystem, where they could be an "invasive" species

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Look for a safely-worded answer being supported by the 2nd paragraph.

choices.text: Such pollution is problematic primarily because of the genetic mutations it would cause in wild fish that live near fish farms.
choices.tag: Too Strong: primarily / Out of Scope: mutations
choices.explanation: The author never singled out one thing as the ****primary**** reason that pollution is a problem, nor does the 2nd paragraph talk about genetic mutations at all.

choices.text: Such pollution contributes to coastal degradation more than any other type of pollution.
choices.tag: Too Strong: more than any other
choices.explanation: We know that pollution from fish farming can result in coastal degradation, but we can't support the hyperbolic statement that it does more coastal degradation ****than any other**** type of pollution.

choices.text: Such pollution is less likely to occur if fish farming enterprises do not pursue intensive production methods.
choices.explanation:
The first sentence of the 2nd paragraph indicates that "the ****more intensive**** forms of fish farming, oriented towards high-volume production, threaten fisheries through water pollution". The following sentence continues talking about the polluting results of "****Intensive**** fish farming".

Since the author emphasized that subtype of fish farming as a source of pollution, we can support the idea that ****less intensive**** forms would be less likely to result in pollution.

This style of correct answer we refer to as *Flipping the Causal Difference-Maker*.

If a sentence in the text emphasizes a causal factor (e.g. "Ted was late to the party, ****because**** he took surface streets"), then a correct answer on a Most Supported task will often sound like, "Ted would have been more likely to be on time if he hadn't taken surface streets".

choices.text: Such pollution cannot be prevented by fish farmers alone without the involvement of government agencies.
choices.explanation: There's nothing in the passage as strong as this claim, which says that "Government agencies ****must**** be involved, or else fish farmers will invariably cause pollution."

choices.text: Such pollution is, however harmful, unlikely to prevent fish farming from eventually relieving the pressure on wild fishery stocks.
choices.explanation:
The author's main point in this passage is a healthy dose of skepticism that fish farming ultimately relieves the pressure on wild fishery stocks.

Her previous sentence (the thesis at the end of paragraph 1) is saying that "Fish farming is a possible solution, ****but also a potential contributing factor****, to the continued decline of ocean fishery stocks."

The first sentence of the 2nd paragraph is saying that "intense fish farming ****threatens the sustainability of ocean fisheries**** through water pollution", which again suggests the opposite of what this answer choice is saying.

passages.title: Accomplice Witnesses And Jailhouse Informants
passages.text:
Criminal courts frequently rely on accomplice witnesses (witnesses who testify regarding the role of an alleged co-conspirator in a crime) and jailhouse informants (witnesses who provide testimony based on information obtained while incarcerated) for prosecutorial information. Typically the testimony provided by such cooperating witnesses includes information garnered through the witnessesʼ conversations with the accused, which can include a purported confession to the crime.

Information from a cooperating witness is often provided in exchange for a reduced sentence or some other incentive. This kind of inducement creates a situation that is highly conducive to evidence fabrication on the part of the cooperating witness. In fact, one recent study concluded that lying informants are rarely prosecuted and therefore have much to gain and little to lose by testifying falsely.

While courts have recognized the unreliable nature of evidence obtained through bartered testimony, they have held that safeguards are in place to adequately protect the accused against a conviction based on false testimony. These safeguards allow effective cross-examination of a cooperating witness and enable the jury to consider a witnessʼs motivations. However, these safeguards do not always provide protection. There are cases in which prosecutors merely imply to cooperating witnesses that they will receive an incentive in exchange for testimony. In such cases, the exchange between prosecution and witness does not have to be disclosed to the jury.

In addition, psychological research on confession testimony—confessions obtained by investigators directly from the accused—reveal further problems with bartered testimony. This research indicates that jurors give undue weight to confession evidence when rendering guilt decisions. This effect is especially notable in cases where jurors are aware that a defendant has been offered an incentive in exchange for a confession. This is particularly relevant here because if people have difficulty realizing the effect that an incentive can have on a defendantʼs behavior, they may also fail to realize the effect that an incentive may have on a cooperating witnessʼs behavior.

A common psychological phenomenon may account for jurorsʼ superficial examination of confession evidence. Studies show that people tend to explain the behavior of others in terms of internal dispositions or attitudes as opposed to external, situational factors. In one study, regardless of whether confession evidence was obtained via negative pressure (threats of worse treatment and/or harsher punishment) or positive pressure (promises of better treatment and/or leniency), mock jurors viewed a confession as evidence that the defendant committed the crime because “only a guilty person would confess to such a crime.” The same logic can be applied to the testimony of cooperating witnesses: jurors may presuppose that accomplice witnesses and jailhouse informants offer their testimony as atonement rather than deducing that external factors made it expedient to give the testimony.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The risks and unreliability of using cooperating witnesses (accomplice witnesses and jailhouse informants) in criminal trials, especially due to incentives for their testimony.

**Framework**

Problem / Solution

**Main Point**

Testimony from cooperating witnesses, which is often incentivized, is unreliable and can lead to false convictions because jurors and courts do not consistently recognize or adjust for the influence that these incentives have on witness and defendant behavior. (The most valuable encapsulating thought is found early in paragraph 2: "This kind of inducement creates a situation that is highly conducive to evidence fabrication on the part of the cooperating witness.")

**P1: Introduction to Cooperating Witnesses**

The passage starts by introducing two common types of cooperating witnesses in criminal cases—accomplice witnesses and jailhouse informants—whose testimony often involves supposed confessions from the accused.

**P2: The Problem with Incentivized Testimony**

Explains that witnesses are often motivated by incentives like reduced sentences, which can encourage them to fabricate evidence. Since lying informants are rarely punished, they have a strong incentive to provide false testimony.

**P3: Judicial Safeguards and Their Limitations**

Highlights that although courts claim safeguards (like cross-examination and disclosure of incentives) exist to protect the accused, these are not always effective. Sometimes, deals between prosecutors and witnesses are implied rather than explicit, so juries are left unaware.

**P4: Jurors' Overreliance on Confession Evidence**

Draws on psychological research to show that jurors often give too much credibility to confession evidence, even when it’s obtained through dubious incentives. If jurors don’t see how incentives affect defendants, they’re likely also blind to how incentives affect witnesses.

**P5: Why Jurors Misjudge Motivations**

Describes a psychological bias where people blame confessions/testimony on internal guilt rather than external incentives. Studies show that, regardless of the methods used to obtain a confession, jurors tend to believe only guilty people would confess—an attitude that similarly influences how they interpret incentivized testimony from witnesses.
